newsitem.title: USA: California voters will get say on all local taxes.
newsitem.headline: California voters will get say on all local taxes.

text.p: Californian voters approved an initiative requiring that all local taxes be submitted to voters for approval despite warnings that the measure would undermine local government finances.
With 100 percent of precincts reporting, Proposition 218 had the support of 56.4 percent of voters, while 43.6 percent were opposed, state election officials said Wednesday.

The measure will make it more difficult for counties and other local governments to raise fees, assessments and taxes. Already at the bottom of the political food chain, California counties and other local governments could lose precious revenue and be forced to slash services, opponents said.

Known as the Right to Vote on Taxes Act, Proposition 218 has shaken elected officials in California and municipal analysts on Wall Street. The California Society of Municipal Analysts has warned that the tax measure could have negative credit implications for some local government bond issues.

Jonathan Coupal, who helped to draft Proposition 218 for the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, said bond firms were exaggerating its negative implications. "The world won't come to an end. It won't," Coupal, director of legal affairs for the association, said.

Proposition 218 was designed to close loopholes in Proposition 13, also spearheaded by activists with the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association. The passage of Proposition 13 in 1978 rolled back local property taxes and curtailed drastically the ability of counties to raise revenue to cover expenses. It also set off a wave of tax-reduction efforts across the country.

Proposition 218, which would apply to all cities, counties, special districts, redevelopment agencies and school districts in the state, would strengthen existing law to require that all new local taxes be submitted to voters for approval. It would also allow property owners to approve new assessments and strictly limit the use of fees and charges.

Coupal, a California legislative analyst, estimated that the measure would reduce local revenues by about $100 million a year. Opponents of the tax measure say the reduction will be significantly greater.
